guides.title: Signalling for Rescue
guides.summary: SOS, mirror, ground signals, whistle and light.

sections.heading: SOS
sections.body:
The international distress signal is three short, three long, three short — · · · — — — · · · — sent as one unbroken character rather than as the three separate letters S, O and S. That detail is not pedantry. In standard Morse the gap between letters is three time units, and if you insert those gaps you have sent "S O S", which a trained ear hears as three ordinary letters that might mean anything at all. Run together with only the normal one-unit spacing between elements, the nine-element burst has no equivalent anywhere in the alphabet, which is exactly why it was chosen. Telegraphists write it with a bar over the top to mark it as a single prosign rather than a word.

Morse timing is proportional, not absolute, so you may send it fast or slow provided you keep the ratios. One unit is whatever you decide it is; half a second is comfortable for a whistle or a torch. A dot is one unit of sound or light, a dash is three, the gap between elements inside the character is one, and the pause before you repeat the whole thing should be at least seven units — in practice three to five seconds, so the pattern reads as a discrete package instead of a continuous stutter. At half-second units one complete SOS runs about fifteen seconds including the closing pause. Send it, then stop and listen or watch for a full minute before sending again. You cannot hear a reply over your own whistle, and blowing straight through the answer you were waiting for is one of the most common ways a good signal is wasted.

Any medium carries it. A whistle, a torch, a car horn, a mirror flash, a pot struck with a rock, a beam interrupted by your cupped hand, a stone banged against a steel pipe or a scaffolding upright inside a collapsed building — the pattern is the message and the medium only has to be capable of being switched on and off. You need no other Morse to use it. Searchers trained in mountain, water and urban rescue recognise the cadence on sight, and even an untrained observer registers that it is not random by the second repetition.

Beneath SOS sits an older and simpler convention: three of anything, evenly spaced, means distress. Three fires, three gunshots, three whistle blasts, three flashes. It works because natural processes rarely produce three deliberately even repetitions, so the evenness itself reads as intent. The conventional acknowledgement is two of anything — two answering blasts or flashes meaning "heard you, stay where you are." Learn both halves of that exchange. Knowing that two blasts is an answer, not another lost party, is what stops you abandoning a good signal position to go looking for the person who has just found you.

sections.heading: Use the app
sections.body:
Open the Tools screen for an automatic SOS strobe that drives the camera flash in the correct three-short, three-long, three-short cadence, together with a loud alarm tone. Both run entirely offline, with no network and no server involved, because a signalling tool that stops working the moment the bars disappear is useless in precisely the situation it exists for.

Then the honest engineering. A phone's camera flash is a single small LED behind a wide diffuser, designed to light a face at two metres, not to be seen from a ridge. Typical output is on the order of tens of lumens spread across a broad angle, against the few hundred focused lumens of even a modest torch. What redeems it is the pattern rather than the power: a rhythmic flash is picked up by peripheral night vision at intensities where a steady point of the same brightness goes unnoticed, so the strobe cadence is doing more work than the raw output is. Point the back of the phone at your target and hold it steady rather than waving it about. A wide-angle emitter that is swinging around spends most of its light on empty sky.

Battery is the constraint that decides everything else. Leave the handset in aeroplane mode between attempts. A phone with no usable tower will ramp its transmitter to maximum power and keep hunting for one, and that search — not the screen, not the flash — is what flattens a battery overnight in a dead zone. Lithium cells also lose usable capacity in cold: near 0 °C you may see roughly half the runtime you would at room temperature, and much of that loss is recoverable, so a phone that has apparently died in the cold will often come back after twenty minutes inside your jacket against your torso. Sustained strobing heats the LED and the phone will thermally throttle or cut the flash entirely, so run it in bursts of a minute or two rather than continuously.

Reserve enough charge for the things only a phone can do. An emergency call to 112, 999 or 911 will attempt to connect over any carrier's network, not only your own, and on most handsets works without a SIM fitted. Some regions support text messaging to emergency services, which can get through on a link too weak to hold a voice call. Recent handsets add satellite emergency messaging that works with no terrestrial coverage at all, though it usually requires a clear view of the sky and patient aiming. A phone that still holds fifteen percent when a searcher's repeater finally comes within range is worth far more than a phone that spent that fifteen percent strobing at an empty valley at three in the morning.

sections.heading: Signal mirror
sections.body:
A signal mirror is the highest-leverage object in a survival kit per gram. It needs no battery, weighs around 30 g, and on a clear day a flash from a good 5 by 7 cm mirror can be seen at distances measured in tens of kilometres. The reason is that it is not producing light but redirecting sunlight: the reflected beam leaves the glass carrying something close to the sun's own surface brightness, so what an observer catches is momentarily comparable to a welding arc set down in the landscape. That beam diverges only slightly, spreading to perhaps a fifteen to twenty metre spot at a kilometre and a half, and that is the whole difficulty — intensely bright, very narrow, and if it is not landing on the target it is landing on nothing.

Aiming is therefore the entire skill. Hold the mirror close under one eye. Extend the other arm and make a V with two fingers, framing the aircraft, boat or vehicle between them. Tilt the mirror until the bright spot of reflected sunlight sits on your fingers: where the spot is, the beam is going. Slide the spot across the gap between the fingers and you have swept the beam across the target. A purpose-made sighting mirror does the same job optically — a retroreflective mesh in the centre shows a small bright dot when the beam is on axis, so you simply move the mirror until that dot sits on the target seen through the aperture.

Sweep even when you can see nothing. Aircraft and vessels pick up mirror flashes at ranges where you cannot make them out at all, and standard practice on open water or above the treeline is to sweep the horizon slowly and continuously whenever the sun is up. A deliberate flash held on a target for a second or two, repeated three times, is far more legible than frantic wobbling. Flash an approaching search aircraft, and flash it again as it passes — but stop flashing a helicopter that is on final approach into your position, because at close range you are simply dazzling the person trying to land.

Improvise when you must. A phone screen at full brightness is a poor mirror, but the rear camera glass, a polished metal panel, a disc's data side, a watch face, a tin lid, a knife blade, a foil wrapper smoothed flat over card, even still water in a dark container will all throw a usable flash, and any of them can be aimed with the two-finger method. The honest limits: a mirror needs a source, and haze, overcast or a sun low behind the target degrades it sharply. Degraded is not useless, and putting the mirror away the instant a cloud crosses discards a tool that is still working at reduced range. Moonlight is not bright enough. After dark the mirror is dead weight and the torch becomes your instrument.

sections.heading: Ground-to-air
sections.body:
Symbols laid out on the ground are the only signal that keeps working while you sleep, while you are unconscious, and while you are half a kilometre away fetching water. They are passive, they are permanent, and they cost nothing but effort, which makes them the first thing to build once shelter is handled.

Size and contrast decide whether they read at all. Make each symbol at least 3 m across — international civil aviation guidance sets a floor of roughly 2.5 m and bigger is strictly better — with strokes broad enough not to dissolve at distance, on the order of a fifth of the symbol's height. Leave at least 3 m of clear ground between adjacent symbols so they do not merge into a single blob from above. Contrast is against the actual backdrop rather than in the abstract: dark boughs or a trampled trench read on snow, pale rocks or bleached driftwood read on dark soil, and a silver emergency blanket that vanishes on a snowfield throws a hard glint on a gravel bar.

The trick that makes a symbol visible when colour contrast is simply unavailable is shadow. Stamp or dig the outline 20 to 30 cm deep and a low sun fills it with a hard black line for hours at each end of the day; pile the spoil along one edge and you double the effect, since the ridge casts as well as the trench. Whatever you use, anchor it. A tarp or a line of clothing that a night wind or a helicopter's rotor downwash rearranges into an unreadable heap is worse than nothing, because you will not know it has gone.

The code itself is deliberately tiny, because searchers have to recognise it instantly from a moving aircraft. The five symbols in current international use are V for "require assistance," X for "require medical assistance," N for "no" or negative, Y for "yes" or affirmative, and an arrow for "proceeding in this direction" — that last being the one to lay if you are forced to abandon the site, pointing the way you have gone. Older military and maritime survival manuals carry a longer table, including F for food and water, LL for "all is well," and II for medical supplies. Those are worth knowing, but they are not what a modern civilian search crew trains on, so lay a V or an X unless you have a specific reason to do otherwise.

If you remember none of the code, an X or the letters SOS spelled out in three-metre characters will be understood by anybody who sees them. Once a symbol is down, stay near it. A search is run outward from a last known position, and a crew that finds a signal with nobody at it must spend time deciding whether they are looking at a live casualty or at yesterday's camp. sections.heading: Fire and Smoke: Signals You Build Before You Need Them
sections.body:
A signal fire only works if it is already half-built when you need it. A search aircraft flying a grid at 90 to 120 knots and three to five hundred feet holds any given patch of ground in view for a few seconds; by the time you have heard the engine, scrambled for kindling and coaxed a flame, it has banked onto its next leg. Prepare three lays in a triangle, or a straight line if the terrain forces it, spaced roughly 25 to 30 m apart. Three rather than one, because a single fire reads to a searcher as somebody's campsite, while three evenly spaced fires are one of the oldest recognised distress patterns there is — older than any radio protocol and understood without language. Build each with a dry tinder-and-kindling core you can light in seconds, then cap it with a breathable cover of bark slabs, turf or boughs that sheds rain and strips off in a single motion.

What you burn next depends on what is behind you, and the chemistry is straightforward. Black smoke is unburnt carbon: starve a flame of oxygen, or feed it something carbon-rich and slow to vaporise such as rubber, plastic or an oil-soaked rag, and the flame breaks the fuel down faster than it can oxidise it, throwing soot. White smoke is mostly steam and condensed volatiles: pile green boughs, damp moss or fresh grass onto a hot bed and the water flashes off as a dense pale column. So against a pale winter sky, snow or open water you want black; against dark conifer canopy or wet rock you want white. A hiker with a broken ankle a mile off-trail, hearing an engine for the first time in six hours, gets one real chance before the sound fades over the ridge and no time whatever to experiment — she needs to already know which pile she reaches for.

Smoke has a weather envelope, and ignoring it wastes the fire. In wind much above 15 knots the column shears apart within a few metres and is effectively invisible from above; in those conditions the flame itself, or a mirror, is the better instrument. Calm mornings under a temperature inversion are ideal, because the inversion caps the column and holds it as a flat visible layer instead of letting it disperse. At night the flame is the signal and the smoke contributes nothing, so switch fuels accordingly.

Two cautions. Burning synthetics releases genuinely toxic combustion products, so stay upwind and never stand in the plume to tend it. And clear bare ground at least 3 m around each lay before you light anything: a signal fire that becomes a wildfire has replaced your rescue with a far larger emergency and, in many jurisdictions, with a liability. Keep the signal lays separate from the fire you cook and warm yourself on, so that you are never forced to tend both at the same moment.

sections.heading: Whistle Blasts and the Rule of Three
sections.body:
Your voice is a bad rescue tool. Shouting projects in one direction at a time, degrades fast — an hour of intermittent yelling can leave you hoarse or voiceless exactly when you need to answer a searcher's call — and it costs breath, water and body heat you may not be able to spare. A pealess emergency whistle, the kind with no cork ball inside to swell, freeze or jam, needs almost no breath to sound, radiates in every direction at once, and produces roughly 100 to 120 decibels at a metre. In good conditions that carries well over a kilometre across open ground or water, considerably further than anyone can effectively shout.

The physics is worth understanding, because it tells you when the whistle will fail. Sound spreads spherically, so intensity falls by about 6 dB for every doubling of distance: a 110 dB whistle is down near 50 dB at a kilometre, roughly the level of ordinary conversation, which is why it still works in quiet country and why it disappears beside a river or in a stiff wind. Most emergency whistles are tuned near 3 to 4 kilohertz, which sits close to the ear's most sensitive band and cuts through the low-frequency rumble of wind and water. The trade-off is that high frequencies are absorbed and scattered by foliage far more than low ones, so a whistle that carries two kilometres over a lake may manage three hundred metres in dense timber.

The pattern matters as much as the volume. Three of anything, evenly spaced, is internationally recognised as distress, independent of language or radio code, and it works precisely because nature does not produce three deliberately even intervals. The conventional reply is two of anything: two answering blasts mean "we hear you, stay where you are," closing the loop without either party needing a radio. Blow three, then stop and listen for a full thirty to sixty seconds. You cannot hear an answer through your own whistle, and people routinely blow straight over the reply they have been waiting hours for.

Carry it where a fall cannot take it from you. A whistle in the lid pocket of a pack is useless if the pack goes down the slope or is swept off a crossing; on a lanyard round your neck or clipped to a shoulder strap it stays with you. Many pack sternum-strap buckles have a whistle moulded into them, which is worth knowing before you need it, and worth testing, since some are little more than decoration.

Picture two hikers who lose sight of each other in fog on a ridgeline with fifteen metres of visibility. Shouting names into the mist gets swallowed by the wind and by the fog's own absorption. Three sharp blasts every thirty seconds cuts through both — and when two blasts come back from below and to the left, each of them now has a bearing to walk on instead of a guess.

sections.heading: Flares and Pyrotechnic Signals
sections.body:
A flare buys a very short, very bright window, and you get very few of them, so spending one badly — too early, aimed wrong, fired when nobody could possibly be looking — means having one fewer for the moment that counts. Handheld flares burn for roughly 60 to 90 seconds at temperatures in the region of 1,200 to 1,600 °C, hot enough to drip molten slag, so hold one at arm's length, downwind, angled away from your body, your boat and any dry vegetation. A synthetic sleeve can melt from radiant heat alone without ever touching the flame. Gloves and eye protection if you have them; over water, hold it out beyond the gunwale so the slag falls into the sea rather than into the bilge.

Aerial parachute flares are a different instrument entirely. They loft a burning candle to something like 300 m and let it descend under a small parachute for 25 to 40 seconds, radiating on the order of 30,000 candela, and on a clear night they are visible for twenty nautical miles or more precisely because they are elevated above the terrain and the horizon that block a ground-level light. Daylight inverts the problem: a flare competes with the sun and largely loses, which is what orange smoke is for. A handheld or floating smoke canister puts out a dense orange plume for one to three minutes and is the correct daytime choice.

Two points matter enough to state plainly. Never aim a flare, handheld or aerial, toward an aircraft, a wheelhouse or a person. A pilot dazzled by a flare in their flight path is a hazard rather than a rescue, and in several jurisdictions this has been prosecuted as interference with aircraft. And flares expire: approved marine pyrotechnics typically carry a service life of about 42 months from manufacture, and time-expired units misfire or fail to ignite at exactly the wrong moment. Replace them on schedule. Expired flares are hazardous waste rather than household rubbish, and many coastguard or fire services run disposal amnesties; never fire an old one for practice, because every unexplained flare sighting launches a real search with real people in it.

Time your shots to your audience. Fire when you have concrete reason to think someone can see it — a vessel on the horizon, an engine growing louder rather than fainter, a known shipping lane at dusk. If you hold several, fire one and wait a minute or two before the second: a pair separated by a deliberate gap confirms to a distant observer that the first was not a trick of the eye, whereas three fired within ten seconds convey no more information than one and empty the locker in a single moment.

There is now a non-pyrotechnic alternative. Electronic visual distress signal devices are LED units that flash an approved distress pattern and, in some regulatory regimes, satisfy the night signalling requirement with no fire risk, no expiry date and no disposal problem. They cannot match a parachute flare's altitude or reach, so treat them as a complement rather than a replacement.

sections.heading: Night Signaling with Flashlights and Strobes
sections.body:
After dark a light beats fire and mirror both, because you do not have to build it or aim it against a sun that has already gone. Night vision runs on the retina's rod cells, which are far more sensitive than cones but carry no colour and are concentrated away from the centre of the retina. That is why a faint light is often easier to see slightly off to one side than by staring straight at it, and why searchers are trained to scan across a sector rather than fix on it. Rods are also very good at detecting change: a flashing source is registered at the edge of vision at intensities where a steady one of identical output goes unnoticed, so a strobe is worth several times its raw lumens. If your torch has no strobe setting, make one by cupping and uncupping your hand over the lens about twice a second, or simply send the SOS cadence of three short, three long, three short.

Beam pattern matters more than headline brightness. A 300-lumen torch with a tight reflector may throw a usable beam two hundred metres; a 1,000-lumen floodlight designed for camp chores spreads the same energy over so wide a cone that it washes out at a fraction of that distance. For signalling you want throw, and throw must be aimed — sweep slowly across the horizon, then hold on any light, window or vessel you find and send the pattern into it rather than past it.

Some cheap tricks work disproportionately well. A chemical light stick tied to half a metre of cord and swung in a circle produces a bright ring, sometimes called a buzz saw, that is visible much further than the stick alone and is unmistakably artificial, and it needs no battery at all. A head torch left on strobe and propped facing the likeliest line of approach keeps signalling while you sleep. A vehicle's hazard lights, dome light or horn will carry the same three-count pattern.

Two cautions close this out. Do not shine a bright light at a helicopter on approach: crews frequently fly on night-vision goggles, which amplify light enormously, and a torch in the face at that moment can blind the pilot at the worst possible second. Point your light at them until they clearly acknowledge, then drop it to the ground or onto your intended landing area. And manage your power deliberately. Alkaline cells lose most of their usable capacity below about −10 °C while lithium primaries hold up far better in cold, so keep spares in an inside pocket against your body, run the light in bursts rather than continuously, and remember that a torch flattened by being left on all night is precisely the torch you needed at four in the morning when the boat finally came past.

sections.heading: Why Some Signals Get Seen and Others Don't
sections.body:
Search crews are not looking for you specifically. They are pattern-matching against a chaotic natural background, at speed, usually from a moving platform, with each observer responsible for a sector and perhaps a second or two of dwell time on any patch of ground before it slides past the window. Search planners quantify this. Every combination of target, terrain and weather has a sweep width — the effective band either side of the track within which a searcher is likely to detect an object — and a probability of detection that is well below certainty on any single pass. That is why searches fly repeated, offset passes, and why anything you do to widen your own sweep width pays compound interest. Three things do it faster than raw size ever will: contrast, motion and geometry.

Contrast means colour against backdrop, not colour in the abstract. Blaze orange is a poor choice against orange sandstone and an excellent one against green forest or blue water. A silver emergency blanket is nearly invisible on snow and throws a hard specular glint against dark rock or wet soil. Earth tones and the muted colours fashionable in outdoor clothing are, seen from the air, camouflage. Know the terrain before you decide what to wear, wave or lay out, and remember that at dawn and dusk a low sun turns any raised object into a long shadow, which is frequently more visible than the object casting it.

Motion matters because the visual system flags movement against a static field before it consciously resolves shape or colour; the reflex is fast and largely involuntary. A brightly coloured jacket waved overhead in a slow, wide arc reads from a passing aircraft in a way the identical garment laid flat on the ground never will. Slow and large beats fast and small — a frantic little wave looks like vegetation moving in the wind, whereas a two-metre arc with the arms fully extended looks like nothing else out there.

Geometry is the quiet one. Nature does not produce straight lines, right angles or perfect circles at any scale visible from the air: rivers meander, treelines are ragged, rockfalls are chaotic. A tarp pulled into a hard-edged triangle, an X stamped into snow, three fires in an even line — each reads as artificial the instant a scanning eye crosses it, precisely because nothing else in the frame looks like that.

Combine all three and you have made yourself the one thing in the grid that does not belong, which is exactly the point. Then hold position. Detection is only half the problem: crews search outward from a last known point, and a signal found with nobody near it is ambiguous evidence that costs them time they were spending on you.

sections.heading: Signaling Mistakes That Have Cost Real Rescues
sections.body:
A handful of errors recur in after-action reviews of search efforts, and every one of them is avoidable with a little forethought.

The most common is timing: gathering fire material only after hearing an aircraft. Given how briefly a search plane holds any one position in view, that is almost always too late. Build the lay in the hour you realise you are in trouble, so that lighting it is a five-second action rather than a ten-minute scramble.

The second is treating a mirror as a bright-sun-only tool. It does need a source, and haze or heavy overcast cuts its range sharply, but reduced is not zero, and putting it away the moment a cloud crosses discards something still working.

The third is firing every flare at once, out of panic or a sense that more must be better. A flare's window is measured in seconds; three fired inside ten seconds convey no more than one, and you have spent the whole locker on a single moment instead of across the several occasions when you were most likely to be seen.

The fourth is building one of anything. A single fire, a single wave, a single laid-out garment is exactly what a searcher expects from ordinary human activity. Three is what tips it from someone camping into someone in trouble, and the extra ten minutes of setup is worth it, because a search that passes you by rarely circles back.

The fifth is leaving. Every hour you walk, the area a team must cover grows roughly with the square of the distance travelled, which is why the standing advice once overdue is to stay put, and why moving off most often turns a one-day search into a week. If you must move, leave a note and a ground arrow pointing the way you have gone, and mark the route behind you.

The sixth is signalling and then hiding. People build a fine signal, then shelter under a tarp out of the wind and never hear the aircraft, or hear it and cannot get outside in the few seconds available. Sleep with the whistle and torch on your body, and site the shelter so you can be out in the open in one movement.

The seventh is the phone left hunting for a tower. A handset with no coverage transmits at full power looking for one and will be flat by morning. Aeroplane mode, broken deliberately at intervals to check, preserves the battery for the moment coverage actually exists.

The eighth precedes all of them: nobody was looking. No signal helps if no search has begun. Leave a trip plan with a specific named person — route, vehicle, expected return, and the hour at which they should call for help — because the interval between overdue and reported is the single largest variable in the outcome, larger than any piece of equipment you can buy. And the mirror image of all of it: casual false alarms erode the response you will get when it is real, and divert crews who are at that moment somebody else's only chance.

sections.heading: Where the SOS Came From: A Short History of Distress Signaling
sections.body:
Long before radio, distress signalling was a relay problem solved optically. In 1792 the French engineer Claude Chappe built a chain of hilltop towers fitted with movable wooden arms — an optical telegraph — able to pass a coded message from Paris to Lille, about 230 km, in minutes rather than the day a rider needed. Navies built their own versions soon after; the British Royal Navy formalised flag semaphore in the early 1800s, and two-flag hand semaphore, with arm positions mapped to letters, remained standard maritime practice well into the twentieth century.

Morse code came later, developed by Samuel Morse and Alfred Vail in the 1830s and 40s for the electric telegraph, and it was that dot-and-dash alphabet, rather than any new invention, that got repurposed for wireless distress decades afterwards. Early operators used CQD — the general call CQ plus D for distress, a Marconi company convention from 1904 — while other national practices used other sequences entirely, and the resulting confusion was exactly the problem the 1906 Berlin International Radiotelegraph Convention set out to fix. It adopted a single standard, effective in 1908: three dots, three dashes, three dots. SOS officially stands for nothing at all; "Save Our Souls" is a later backronym. It was chosen because the pattern is unmistakable and nearly impossible to send wrong by a shaking or inexperienced hand, which is precisely what you want from a signal transmitted under duress. When RMS Titanic went down in 1912 her senior wireless operator Jack Phillips sent both codes — the older CQD out of habit and the newer SOS — in one of the signal's first widely publicised uses.

"Mayday," the voice equivalent, is younger still. It was coined in 1923 by Frederick Stanley Mockford, a senior radio officer at Croydon Airport near London, who needed a spoken word instantly recognisable to English and French speakers working traffic across the Channel; he chose it to echo the French m'aidez, "help me." The lesser-known "Pan-pan," from the French panne meaning breakdown, signals urgency short of grave and imminent danger, and is the correct call for a serious problem that is not yet life-threatening.

The Morse era ended at sea on 1 February 1999, when the Global Maritime Distress and Safety System replaced manual watchkeeping with automated digital selective calling and satellite alerting. Its centrepiece is the 406 MHz distress beacon — an EPIRB at sea, an ELT in aircraft, a PLB carried personally — registered to a named owner and detected by the international Cospas-Sarsat satellite constellation, which made its first rescue in 1982. Modern beacons embed a satellite position and are typically located within tens of metres in minutes. Satellite monitoring of the older analogue 121.5 MHz beacons was switched off in February 2009. The old patterns still matter when a beacon fails or was never carried, but the beacon is now the first thing to reach for.

sections.heading: Equipment Worth Carrying for Signaling
sections.body:
Signalling gear earns its place by covering different failure modes rather than by being individually excellent. Build the kit across modalities — audible, reflective, luminous and chromatic — because each one fails in conditions where another still works. A mirror is dead at night and weak under heavy overcast; a torch dies with its battery; a whistle is swallowed beside a river or in dense timber; bright colour does nothing in fog. Carry at least one item that needs no power at all, because cold and water take batteries first and take them without warning.

Weight is not the constraint people assume it is. A whistle, a sighting mirror, a couple of light sticks, a small torch and a blaze-coloured stuff sack together come to something like 250 to 350 g and cost less than a night's accommodation. The real constraint is where they live. Anything that matters has to be on your body — a jacket pocket, a neck lanyard, a belt loop — and not in the pack, because packs are precisely what get dropped down a slope, swept off a river crossing, or left at a camp you cannot get back to.

One honest note that a purely analogue kit cannot cover: a registered 406 MHz personal locator beacon, or a satellite messenger, outperforms every item here by a wide margin, alerting a coordinated rescue service with your coordinates in minutes instead of depending on somebody happening to look your way. If you spend money on one thing, spend it there — and carry the analogue kit anyway, because it is what still works when the beacon is at the bottom of the river with the pack.
ingredients: A pealess emergency whistle (look in the camping/outdoor section of any sporting-goods or hardware store) — the ball-less design won't jam or freeze, unlike a traditional referee's whistle.

A glass or polycarbonate signal mirror with an aiming hole or grid in the center, sold in the camping or marine-safety aisle of an outdoor retailer — a household pocket mirror or a phone screen works in a pinch but lacks the aiming aperture.
A small pack of chemical light sticks from a camping or emergency-supply store, useful as a passive night marker that needs no battery or aim.
A compact, far-throwing LED flashlight or headlamp with a strobe setting, available at any hardware or outdoor store — look for stated lumen output and beam distance, not just price.

A brightly colored, high-contrast item — an orange or blaze-pink stuff sack, bandana, or emergency space blanket from a camping store — chosen for contrast against the terrain you'll actually be in, not just visibility in a store aisle.
A reliable fire-starting kit (ferro rod, waterproof matches, or a lighter plus dry tinder) from any camping or hardware store, kept somewhere it won't get wet.

USCG-approved handheld and aerial flares from a marine-supply or boating store, if you'll be near water — check the stamped expiration date before every trip and replace expired ones rather than keeping them as a backup.

sections.heading: Step-by-Step: Rehearse Your Signals Before You're Desperate
sections.body:
Signalling looks trivial written down and is surprisingly hard to execute cold. Under acute stress the body floods with adrenaline, peripheral vision narrows, fine motor control degrades, and complex sequences you have only read about tend to evaporate. What survives is whatever repetition has already converted into a motor program. Aiming a mirror is the clearest case: almost nobody puts a flash onto a moving target on the first attempt without having practised the sighting geometry at least once, and that failed attempt costs the only pass the aircraft was going to give you.

Rehearsal also surfaces the equipment failures you would otherwise discover at the worst possible moment — the whistle whose pea has swollen shut, the torch whose cells corroded over winter, the flare pack whose stamped date expired two seasons ago. Run the drill in daylight, with a partner who can confirm what they actually see, then repeat the light half at dusk. The point is not to prove that the tools work. It is to make the actions automatic enough that a cold, frightened, dehydrated version of you can still perform them. Repeat it once a season and re-check the kit each time.
steps: Pick a partner and two vantage points roughly 300–500 m apart with clear line of sight — opposite ends of a park, a beach, or a ridge and a valley — and bring a signal mirror, a whistle, and a flashlight.

Practice the mirror aim in daylight: hold the mirror close to your eye, extend your other arm and make a V or peace sign with your fingers toward your partner, and tilt the mirror until the sunspot reflected onto your fingers lines up between them — that's the technique that gets a mirror flash actually onto a target instead of scattered nearby. Have your partner confirm by radio or hand signal when they see the flash.

Switch to the whistle: from your two positions, send three evenly-spaced blasts, wait, and have your partner answer with two blasts. Repeat until the timing feels automatic rather than something you have to think through.

At dusk or after dark, repeat the exercise with flashlights: send three short, three long, three short flashes (SOS) toward your partner, and have them flash two short flashes back as acknowledgment before you both walk toward each other's position using only the light as a bearing.

At home, gather your fire-lay materials (tinder, kindling, and both a green/damp and a dry fuel option) and practice building three separate lays, timing yourself — the goal is under two minutes per lay, since that's roughly the reaction window you'll have when you actually hear an aircraft.

If you carry marine flares, do not fire a live one for practice — instead, read the manufacturer's instructions cover to cover and physically rehearse the pull-and-hold or twist-and-strike motion with an unloaded practice unit if your marine-supply store carries one, so your hands know the motion without you ever having discharged a real flare indoors or in an unsafe direction.

guides.title: Calling for Help
guides.summary: Reach emergency services, save battery, improvise signal.

sections.heading: Emergency call
sections.body:
Dial your local emergency number — the SOS screen picks it for your region, but it is worth knowing the map anyway: 911 in the US and Canada, 112 across the EU and on GSM networks in much of the world, 999 in the UK, 000 in Australia. Modern phones translate between them at the network level, so dialling 112 in North America or 911 in Europe still reaches the local service; the number is recognised by the network itself rather than looked up like an ordinary contact. That special handling is why emergency calls behave unlike any other call you make. If your own carrier has no coverage where you stand but a competitor's tower is reachable, the phone is permitted to place the emergency call through the rival network — a phone showing 'emergency calls only' is telling you precisely that. In many countries the call will even go through with no SIM card installed, but know the catch before you rely on it: a SIM-less phone gives the dispatcher no callback number, so a dropped call cannot be returned, and some countries have disabled SIM-less emergency dialling entirely because of hoax misuse. An old drawer phone is a backup, never the plan. The lock screen matters too — every modern phone exposes an Emergency call button below the passcode prompt, so you can dial from anyone's phone, locked or not.

Once connected, give your location first, then stay on the line until the call-taker tells you to hang up. If the call drops, most centres will attempt to ring you back: keep the line free, answer numbers you do not recognise, and resist the urge to start phoning family before help is confirmed — an engaged line at the wrong moment costs real minutes. If you cannot speak safely, do not hang up either; an open line with background noise still reaches a trained call-taker, and many services have procedures for silent calls.

A concrete example of why the routing rules matter: a traveller whose home SIM has no roaming agreement in the country they are driving through sees 'no service' for everything ordinary, yet a crash on the motorway is still one dial away, because the phone may register with whichever local network is strongest for the duration of a 112 call. The reverse trap exists as well: Wi-Fi calling can carry an emergency call in some configurations, but the location the system attaches to a Wi-Fi call can be stale or wrong, so state where you are explicitly rather than trusting the network to know. Finally, remember that a voice call needs a continuous two-way channel — the most demanding thing a phone does with a weak signal. If the audio keeps collapsing into silence, hold the phone still and stay on the exact spot where it connected; if voice fails outright, switch strategy to text rather than redialling endlessly.

sections.heading: If you can't get through
sections.body:
Texts need far less signal than calls, and the reason is structural: a voice call must hold a continuous two-way channel open for minutes, while an SMS is a burst of at most a few hundred bytes that rides the network's signalling channel — the same lightweight channel phones use to register with a tower. A link far too weak to sustain speech can often still land that burst, and the phone keeps retrying an unsent message automatically each time conditions flicker. That changes your tactics in a dead zone: type the message once, press send, then concentrate on giving the phone its best chance — high open ground, line-of-sight toward a town, highway, or visible tower, phone held still above head height. Watch the message status; 'delivered' is your confirmation, but an unmarked message may still be quietly retrying, so give it minutes before moving on.

Make the text itself do the work of a call you cannot place. The SOS screen pre-fills your coordinates; if you are composing by hand, open the compass or maps app and copy the decimal GPS coordinates into the message, then add the minimum a rescuer needs: who is hurt and how badly, what you plan to do next ('staying put at these coordinates'), and when you will try again ('phone on at the top of each hour'). Ask the recipient explicitly to call emergency services and relay the message — do not assume they will infer it — and send the same text to two or three reliable people rather than one, since you cannot know who is near their phone. Every word you pre-position in that message is a word that does not depend on a voice channel ever materialising.

Two honest limits keep expectations calibrated. Delivery can be delayed — a message accepted by the network in a fringe area may sit undelivered for many minutes, and replies may reach you out of order, so do not interpret silence as failure or re-send in a panic loop that burns battery. And an ordinary SMS to a friend is a relay, not a direct line to a dispatcher: it adds a human hop, with all the delay and misunderstanding a hop can add, which is why it is the fallback rather than the first move. A worked example of the form that works: 'Emergency. Fell at 46.8523, -121.7603, right ankle broken, cannot walk. Call 911 and give them these coordinates. Staying put. Phone back on at 3:00.' Short, complete, and useful even if it is the only message that ever gets through.

sections.heading: Pixel satellite SOS
sections.body:
Recent Pixel phones — the Pixel 9 generation onward, in supported regions — can exchange text messages with emergency services via satellite when there is no cell or Wi-Fi signal at all. The mechanism explains every quirk of using it. A phone's transmitter is designed to reach a tower a few kilometres away and is being asked to reach a satellite enormously farther out; the link only closes with a clear, unobstructed view of the sky and the phone aimed correctly. That is why the feature walks you through pointing: the screen shows where the satellite sits, you sweep the phone until it locks, then hold roughly that orientation for the whole exchange. Go to the most open ground available — a meadow, ridge, wide beach, or large clearing. Tree canopy, canyon walls, and buildings on the horizon can each break the link; a slot canyon or dense forest may make satellite messaging impossible until you move, and heavy storm cloud can degrade it.

Expect a different rhythm from ordinary texting. The session opens with a short questionnaire (what happened, who is hurt) precisely because the channel is slow — the answers compress what would take many round-trips into one structured report that reaches the emergency centre along with your location. Each message can take tens of seconds or longer to send, so keep replies short and factual, stay outside, keep the sky view clear, and do not wander mid-exchange. The feature can also notify your emergency contacts. Satellite sessions work the phone hard, so treat battery as part of the plan: warm the phone if it is cold and close everything else first.

Know the boundaries honestly. Availability depends on model, region, carrier and account status, and the service can change over time — confirm that Satellite SOS appears in your phone's Safety settings before you are somewhere that needs it, not after. Where any cell signal exists, an ordinary emergency call is faster and carries far more information; satellite is the last rung, not a preferred channel. And if your life routinely takes you beyond coverage — solo backcountry travel, small-boat passages, remote fieldwork — a dedicated 406 MHz personal locator beacon (PLB) or a subscription satellite messenger still out-earns a phone: a PLB transmits a powerful distress burst to the international COSPAS-SARSAT rescue satellite system, needs no subscription, is registered free to its owner (in the US with NOAA), works in gloved hands, and holds its battery for years. The phone's satellite SOS is a superb backstop you already carry; it is not a replacement for purpose-built rescue hardware.

sections.heading: Wireless emergency alerts
sections.body:
Leave Wireless Emergency Alerts ON (Settings ▸ Safety & emergency) to receive government broadcasts about nearby threats even when data is down. They work when nothing else does because they are not messages addressed to you at all: WEA uses cell broadcast, a one-to-many channel in which the tower transmits a single alert that every compatible phone in range hears simultaneously, the way a radio station reaches every receiver at once. Nothing is queued or delivered individually, which is why alerts cut through the exact congestion that blocks calls and texts during a disaster — a saturated tower that cannot complete your call can still broadcast. It also means the system needs no app, no sign-up, and no data plan, and it learns nothing about you; your phone simply listens.

Targeting is geographic, not personal. Authorities draw the warning area and the towers serving it broadcast the alert, so you receive warnings for wherever you physically are — which is exactly the point when you are travelling through a flash-flood watch you have never heard of. In the US the alerts come in classes: National Alerts (which cannot be switched off), imminent-threat alerts such as tornado and flash-flood warnings, AMBER alerts, and public-safety messages, plus occasional tests. Messages are short — up to a few hundred characters — and arrive with a distinctive penetrating tone and vibration designed to be unmistakable; on most phones the highest-severity alerts sound even with the ringer off. The same cell-broadcast technology underlies the UK's Emergency Alerts, EU-Alert in Europe, and Japan's earthquake early warnings, so a modern phone abroad generally participates in the local system automatically.

Treat an alert as a trigger, not the full story. A few hundred characters can say 'flash flood warning for this area, move to higher ground now', and its arrival at three in the morning — waking you before water reaches the road — is the system doing exactly what it exists to do; the follow-up detail about which roads and which shelters comes from local radio or official channels once you are already acting. Know the honest limits, too: cell broadcast still requires a working tower, so an event that destroys local infrastructure outright can silence WEA along with everything else — that gap is precisely what a battery or hand-crank weather radio covers, since broadcast transmitters sit far from the damage and your radio only receives. And resist the urge to disable alert classes after one annoying test or a distant AMBER alert: the class you silence is chosen before you know what the next alert would have said.

sections.heading: Save the battery
sections.body:
Enable battery saver, lower the screen, and above all stop the phone from hunting. The mechanism that kills a phone in a dead zone is the search itself: when a phone cannot find a tower it escalates, scanning band after band and driving its transmitter toward maximum power in repeated registration attempts, around the clock. A phone hunting for signal in a fringe area drains far faster than the same phone idle with good coverage — which is why airplane mode between deliberate attempts is the single highest-value habit in this guide. The discipline that makes it work is a schedule you can keep under stress: for example, five minutes at the top of every hour — airplane mode off, hold still at your best spot, watch for bars and incoming messages, make your attempt, airplane mode back on. A schedule also makes you predictable to the people trying to reach you: a contact who received your earlier text knows when your phone will be listening, so include the check window in any message you get out.

The screen is the other large consumer in normal use, so set brightness to minimum, shorten the screen timeout, and stop touching the phone between windows — every idle wake costs. Close background apps or use the deepest battery-saver tier (recent Pixels offer an extreme mode that suspends everything nonessential), switch off Bluetooth and Wi-Fi scanning, and use the flashlight in brief signalling bursts, never continuously.

Cold is a separate, sneakier enemy. Lithium-ion chemistry sags below freezing: a phone reading a healthy percentage can shut off abruptly in the cold and revive once warmed, because the gauge reflects charge the chilled cell temporarily cannot deliver. Keep the phone in an inside pocket against your torso, not an outer shell pocket, and warm it before important attempts. If you are topping up from a power bank in freezing conditions, warm the phone first as well — charging a lithium cell below about 0 °C damages it.

Finally, ration with intent. Do not ride the battery to zero: protect a last reserve — think ten to twenty percent — for the moment that matters most, a helicopter overhead or a searcher's shout, when one short call or one bright screen may finish the rescue. Powering fully off saves slightly more than airplane mode, but each boot costs a surge of energy and a dark phone cannot receive the callback you may already have earned; once any message has gone out, airplane mode with scheduled windows is the better default.

sections.heading: Improve reception
sections.body:
Higher ground and clear sky help most, and the physics says why. Cellular signals occupy the UHF range — roughly 600 megahertz to a few gigahertz — where radio behaves more like light than like the AM band: it travels in near-straight lines, bends only weakly over ridges, and is absorbed by water in all its forms, including wet foliage and the water in your own body. From that, the terrain rules follow directly. Valley bottoms, gorges, and dense timber are the worst places to attempt contact; spurs, saddles, and open ridgelines with a sightline toward a town, a highway corridor, or a visible mast are the best. A tower can serve clear line-of-sight out to tens of kilometres, so being able to see distant civilisation is genuinely meaningful — a useful field rule is that if you can see far, you have a chance of being heard.

At the small scale, weak signal is patchy in a way that surprises people: reflections off terrain interfere with the direct path, creating dead spots and live spots literally a step apart. So when one flickering bar appears, stop walking. Plant yourself, raise the phone above head height, hold it still, and make the attempt from exactly there; moving a metre can make or break a fringe connection, and walking while trying reliably drops it. Your grip matters too — modern phones carry their antennas in the frame, so a fist wrapped around the edges, or a phone pressed flat against your chest, absorbs the very signal you need. Hold it loosely near the bottom, or prop it on a rock or pack and use speakerphone.

The folk remedies deserve honest grading. A curved sheet of foil behind the phone acts as a crude reflector and occasionally adds a usable margin; resting the phone on a large metal surface such as a car roof sometimes helps in a similar way. Both are worth sixty seconds; neither substitutes for a hundred metres of elevation. Prefer the edge of a clearing to the middle of dense canopy — a wet canopy overhead is a strong absorber, and conditions improve once rain stops and leaves dry. Fringe coverage also drifts with atmospheric conditions, so a spot that was dead at noon is occasionally alive at night; re-try before concluding a location is hopeless. A worked example ties it together: a hiker in a creek bottom gets nothing, climbs fifteen minutes up the side ridge to a spur with a distant view of the valley town, stands still with the phone held high — and the text queued in the bottomlands quietly reports 'delivered'.

sections.heading: What the Dispatcher Needs to Hear First
sections.body:
Panic compresses time and scrambles the order people naturally give information in — most callers start with what happened ('there's been a crash!') when what a dispatcher actually needs first is where, because location is what determines which units get sent and how fast. Give your location before your story: a street address and cross street if you have one, or a GPS coordinate, mile marker, trailhead name, or specific landmark ('the blue water tower, half a mile past the second switchback on the ridge trail') if you don't. Cell-network location data (Enhanced 911) that reaches the dispatcher automatically is often accurate to only a wide radius, especially in rural or mountainous terrain with sparse tower coverage, so never assume the call center already knows exactly where you are — say it out loud regardless.

After location, the dispatcher needs, in roughly this order: the nature of the emergency (medical, fire, crime, crash), how many people are involved and their condition, and a callback number in case the call drops. Then stay on the line — hanging up the instant you've said your piece is one of the most common mistakes callers make, because dispatchers are often walking you through first-aid instructions or gathering follow-up details (is the patient breathing, is the scene safe to approach) that directly shape what responders bring and how they're briefed en route.

A driver who's just seen a rollover on an unmarked stretch of highway, for instance, is far more useful to a dispatcher saying 'northbound Route 9, about two miles past the county line exit, one vehicle off the road, I can see one person moving inside' than one who opens with 'oh my god, there's been a terrible accident' and has to be walked back to the actual facts a sentence at a time while the clock keeps running.

Two mechanics of the dispatch system are worth knowing because they change how callers behave. First, answering questions does not delay help. In a modern centre, call-taking and dispatching run in parallel: units are typically being alerted from the moment a location and call type are entered, while the call-taker continues gathering detail that is relayed to crews already rolling. Patiently answering 'is he breathing?' is not holding the ambulance back — it is briefing it. Second, protect the callback channel. Once you have called, keep the line free and the ringer on, and answer numbers you do not recognise; if the call drops, most centres attempt to ring back, and an engaged or silenced phone at that moment costs real time. Resist phoning family until help is confirmed on its way. And if you genuinely do not know where you are, do not freeze on the question — reconstruct instead: name the trailhead or junction where you started, the time you set out, the direction you walked, what you can see and hear ('running water to my left, a radio mast on the far ridge'), or read coordinates straight from the phone's compass or maps app. Every fact shrinks the search area, and dispatchers are trained to assemble a location from exactly these fragments.

sections.heading: Texting 911: When It Works and When It Doesn't
sections.body:
Text-to-911 exists specifically for situations where a voice call would make things worse or simply isn't possible: a domestic-violence or home-invasion situation where speaking aloud could alert an attacker, a medical or speech condition that prevents talking, or a deaf or hard-of-hearing caller who communicates by text. It rides over the same cellular SMS channel as an ordinary text message, not mobile data, so it can work with only minimal signal — but coverage is a patchwork rather than a guarantee. Availability depends on whether the local 911 call center has built out text-to-911 infrastructure, and it varies county to county rather than being uniformly available everywhere the way voice 911 is; text the number and, if the system isn't built out in your area, you'll typically get an automated bounce-back telling you to call by voice instead.

When it does work, keep the message short and front-load the same information a voice call needs — location first, since text-to-911 does not reliably carry the same automatic location data as a voice call, then the nature of the emergency in plain language, no abbreviations or slang the dispatcher might not parse under time pressure. And never test the real 911 text system out of curiosity; if you want to confirm text-to-911 is available where you live, call your local non-emergency dispatch line and ask, rather than sending a live text that ties up a dispatcher's attention on a false alarm.

If the situation forces silence, make the whole phone cooperate with the channel: switch off the ringer before you text so an incoming reply cannot betray you, keep the screen dimmed but where you can see it, and keep answering — text-to-911 is a conversation with a call-taker, not a single flare, and the follow-up questions serve the same purpose they would on a voice call. Expect the medium's limits: messages can arrive delayed or out of order, and most centres cannot receive photos, videos, or group messages, so send plain words, from your own number, in one thread. A worked example of the form that works: 'Break-in at 41 Elm St, hiding in upstairs bedroom closet, two intruders downstairs, cannot talk.' Location, situation, where you are inside it, and why you are texting — everything a dispatcher needs, sendable in fifteen silent seconds. For deaf, hard-of-hearing, and speech-disabled callers there is also real-time text (RTT), the modern successor to TTY built into current Android phones: it places an actual call on which characters transmit as you type them, with no send button, so the exchange flows at conversation speed over the voice-call channel itself. Where the carrier and the local call centre support it, RTT reaches emergency services directly — enable and try it in the phone's accessibility settings before the day you need it.

sections.heading: Medical ID: Letting Responders Help You Before You Can Ask
sections.body:
An unconscious or unresponsive person is the worst possible time for a first responder to be locked out of basic medical facts — and by default, a locked phone gives them nothing. Android phones (and the Pixel's own Safety app) let you fill in a Medical Information / Emergency profile that's visible directly from the lock screen's 'Emergency' button, without unlocking the device at all: allergies, current medications, medical conditions, blood type, and one or more emergency contacts a responder can call on the spot.

What actually earns its place in that profile is narrower than 'everything about you.' Allergies matter because a paramedic administering a drug needs to know instantly if it could trigger anaphylaxis. Medications matter most when they change how a condition presents or how it should be treated — a person on blood thinners bleeds differently from a head injury than one who isn't, and that single fact can change a trauma team's first move. Conditions like diabetes, epilepsy, or a heart condition matter because they can explain symptoms (confusion, a seizure, collapse) that would otherwise send responders down the wrong diagnostic path entirely. And an emergency contact who can speak to your medical history or authorize care is worth more here than a long list of casual contacts. Set it up once, and it works for you exactly in the moment you're least able to speak for yourself.

Two refinements push a profile from good to genuinely useful. Be specific where specificity changes treatment: name the anticoagulant rather than writing 'blood thinner', note an insulin pump or continuous glucose monitor, and record implanted hardware — a pacemaker or implanted defibrillator matters to a crew placing defibrillation pads, and a metal implant matters again later at imaging. Then keep the profile current, because a stale entry actively misleads: a medication you stopped a year ago can send treatment down the wrong path as surely as an omission. Re-check it after every prescription change and after every phone upgrade — a new phone starts blank, and this is among the settings most commonly lost in a migration. The honest limit of the whole approach is the hardware it lives on: a phone can be dead, shattered, or thrown clear of a crash. For conditions that change first-response treatment — a severe allergy, insulin-dependent diabetes, epilepsy, anticoagulant therapy — a medical-alert bracelet or necklace remains the standard responders are trained to check for, works at zero battery, and survives what phones do not; the lock-screen profile complements it rather than replacing it. Together they cover exactly the moment described above: a responder kneeling beside someone unresponsive, reading the essentials from a wrist and a lock screen, and phoning a listed contact who can answer the questions the patient cannot.

sections.heading: Two-Way and Amateur Radio When the Towers Are Down
sections.body:
Cellular networks fail in exactly the situations you're most likely to need them — a wildfire taking out a tower, a hurricane knocking out power to a whole region, a stadium's worth of phones overloading a cell site at once. Radio doesn't route through that infrastructure at all, which is why it's worth understanding the tiers below cellular, even though none of them replace calling 911 when that option exists.

FRS (Family Radio Service) handhelds need no license, transmit at up to 2 watts, and in practice manage something like 1–2 km line-of-sight in typical terrain — enough to keep a hiking group or a family at a fair in touch with each other, not enough to reach outside help. GMRS (General Mobile Radio Service) sits one step up: it requires an inexpensive FCC license (no exam, and the license covers your whole household), allows up to 50 watts on some channels, and can reach much farther, especially relayed through a repeater. Amateur ('ham') radio opens the largest range of frequencies and power levels of all, but requires passing an FCC Technician-class licensing exam first — in exchange, licensed operators can reach repeater networks that relay a signal tens or hundreds of kilometers, sometimes farther through atmospheric skip.

The legal line matters: transmitting on GMRS without the license, or on amateur bands without having passed the exam, is against FCC rules in ordinary circumstances. The one carve-out (FCC Part 97.405) is a genuine emergency where no other means of communication is available and life or property is at immediate risk — in that specific case, unlicensed emergency transmission is permitted, but it's an exception built for a true last resort, not a loophole for casual use. One rung below all of this, a hand-crank or battery NOAA Weather Radio needs no license at all and no cellular signal either, because it only receives — it's worth owning purely for the alert broadcasts during the exact kind of event that might take the cell towers down in the first place.

Whatever tier you settle on, the physics rewards height over wattage: these VHF and UHF signals are line-of-sight, so transmitting from a rooftop, ridge, or upper-floor window routinely outperforms doubling power from a basement, and holding the antenna vertical keeps its polarisation matched to the base and repeater antennas listening for you. On or near the water there is one more channel to know: marine VHF channel 16 (156.8 MHz) is the international distress, safety, and calling frequency, monitored by coast guards and large vessels — for coastal boaters a fixed or handheld marine radio on channel 16 is a more dependable rescue path than a phone, and a spoken distress call opens 'Mayday, Mayday, Mayday' followed by the vessel's name, position, the nature of the emergency, and the number of people aboard. Finally, radios only work as a system you have rehearsed: agree a channel and a check-in schedule with your group in advance, and make one real test call before the day it matters, because a family that owns radios but has never keyed them will fumble exactly when fumbling is most expensive.

sections.heading: Building a Family Emergency Communication Plan
sections.body:
During a large regional disaster, long-distance calls routed out of the immediate area often complete before local calls do — every local tower is saturated with everyone in the disaster zone trying to reach someone else in the same disaster zone, while a call routed to a relative three states away rides on network capacity that's untouched. That's the entire logic behind the standard emergency-management advice (used by organizations like the American Red Cross and FEMA) to designate a single out-of-area contact: someone all the separated members of your household call and text with their status, so that person becomes the switchboard relaying 'everyone's safe, we're at the school' back to whoever else checks in, rather than five family members burning phone battery and network capacity trying to reach each other directly across a jammed local grid.

A workable plan needs three things written down somewhere physical, not just saved in a phone that could be dead, lost, or left behind: the out-of-area contact's number, a primary meeting point near home for a sudden local event (a fire, a gas leak), and a secondary meeting point outside the immediate neighborhood for something that makes the primary point unreachable. Make sure kids old enough to use a phone have the out-of-area number memorized or written on a card in their bag, not just stored in a contacts list they may not have access to — and actually rehearse it once, the way you'd rehearse a fire drill, rather than assuming everyone will remember a plan they've only heard described once.

Layer onto that the institutional plans that will override yours: schools do not simply release children during an emergency — they hold or relocate them and release only to adults on the authorised pickup list through a formal reunification process, so keeping that list current is part of your communication plan, and both parents should know the school's stated procedure and relocation site. Workplaces likewise have muster points and accountability procedures worth learning before the day. Picture the plan working: an earthquake at two in the afternoon — parents at workplaces in different directions, children held safely at school, local calls failing. Each parent sends the out-of-area contact a two-line text ('safe, at the office, walking to the school at four'), the contact relays both statuses onward, and nobody improvises into a jammed network, because everyone already knows the next agreed step. Prefer text over voice for these check-ins — a short SMS asks far less of a strained network than repeated call attempts. Then keep the plan alive: walk through it twice a year — the clock changes are an easy anchor — reverify the numbers, reprint the cards, re-brief the kids, and rewrite it after any move, school change, or new household member.

sections.heading: Gear That Keeps You Reachable
sections.body: A communication plan is only as good as the hardware that survives long enough to use it, and the list below is ordered by how much survival each dollar and gram actually buys. Stored power comes first because nearly every failure mode in this guide traces back to a dead battery. A 10,000 mAh bank realistically refills a typical phone about twice — conversion losses eat a meaningful slice of the label figure, which is quoted for the bank's internal cells rather than for what reaches your phone — and that turns a one-day phone into a roughly three-day phone with disciplined use. Solar sits a tier behind, and its honest limit is patience: a small folding panel wants hours of direct, square-on sun, produces little under cloud or canopy, and is best used to refill the bank while you do other things, with the phone then charged from the bank. The car deserves respect as the biggest battery most households own: a vehicle's 12-volt system dwarfs any pocket bank, and idling the engine periodically keeps it topped up while it charges your devices — but only outdoors with the exhaust clear (of snow especially), and never in a garage or any enclosed space, because carbon monoxide kills quietly. The radios and the weather receiver earn their places in the sections above; what this list adds is the discipline of keeping them alive. Everything electronic here decays silently — lithium banks self-discharge over months, stored cells corrode, cables fray or stop matching the phone you carry now — so put the whole kit on a simple maintenance loop: top the bank off regularly, crank or power the radio for a minute every few months, and confirm the spare cable still fits your current phone. The laminated card is listed last and fails never: paper needs no charge, survives a soaking if laminated, and is the one component still working after every battery in the bag is flat.
ingredients: A portable battery bank (10,000+ mAh) from any electronics or hardware store, kept charged and in your bag rather than a drawer — the single highest-value item on this list.
A small solar charging panel, sold alongside camping gear at outdoor and hardware stores, for a multi-day outage where wall power isn't coming back soon.
A car charger or 12V-to-USB adapter, cheap and available anywhere car accessories are sold, since a parked vehicle is often the largest battery you have access to.
A hand-crank or battery-powered NOAA weather radio from an electronics or emergency-supply store — it receives alerts with no cellular signal and no license required.

A GMRS radio pair (with the household FCC license applied for online) or a licensed amateur handheld, available at an electronics or outdoor-recreation store, for keeping in touch with your own group when cellular is down.
A laminated card with your out-of-area contact's number, your family meeting points, and any critical medical information, kept in a wallet or bag — the one item that works with zero battery at all.
A spare charging cable for your specific phone, kept with the battery bank rather than assumed to be wherever your everyday cable is.

sections.heading: Step-by-Step: Set Up Your Emergency Comms This Week
sections.body: Everything above is worth nothing if it is still theoretical the day you need it, so this section converts it into a single week's checklist — most of it under an hour of actual effort. The ordering is deliberate: the tasks that protect you while unconscious and the ones requiring another person's agreement come first, because those cannot be improvised mid-emergency, while gear purchases and licences can trail by a few days without much risk. Apply one principle to every step: do not stop at 'done' — prove it. Lock the phone and confirm the medical profile really shows from the Emergency button; have each family member actually send the out-of-area contact a test text from their own phone; stand at the meeting point once so it is a place you have been rather than an address you have read; key the radio and hear the other handset answer. A plan verified once beats a plan assumed ten times, because verification is where the surprises surface — the blank profile, the mistyped number, the radio still in its packaging. Then defend the work against decay, which is how good preparations actually die: phones get replaced and start blank, contacts move house, kids change schools, counties add text-to-911 support. A recurring reminder every six months to re-run these checks takes about fifteen minutes to satisfy and is the difference between a plan and a memory of one. Finally, spread the work: a plan built by one person is a plan only one person understands, so do the shared steps out loud, together.
steps: Open your phone's emergency/medical ID settings (on Android: Settings → Safety & emergency, or the Pixel Safety app) and fill in allergies, medications, conditions, and at least one emergency contact — check that it's visible from the lock screen without unlocking by locking the phone and tapping 'Emergency' yourself to confirm.

Call one relative or friend who lives outside your immediate region and ask them to be your family's out-of-area contact; save their number under a clearly labeled contact and write it on a physical card for each family member's bag or wallet.

With your household, pick a primary meeting point within your neighborhood and a secondary one farther away, say both out loud together once, and write both addresses on the same card as the out-of-area contact.

Buy or charge a portable battery bank today if you don't have one, and get in the habit of topping it off whenever you charge your phone overnight, so it's never sitting empty when you actually need it.

Call your local non-emergency police or fire dispatch number and ask directly whether text-to-911 is available in your county — do not test it by sending a live text — and note the answer somewhere you'll remember.

If you're considering GMRS or amateur radio, apply for the GMRS license online (no test) or look up your nearest amateur-radio exam session for the Technician license, and once licensed, do one real test call with a family member from two different rooms or vehicles to confirm both radios actually work before you rely on them.

guides.title: Water Rescue Basics: Reach, Throw, Row, Go
guides.summary: The instinct to swim out after a drowning person is one of the most dangerous impulses in outdoor safety. This guide covers the reach-throw-row-go rescue hierarchy, the physiology of cold-water shock, what real drowning actually looks like, and the basics of ice rescue — all built around one idea: help without becoming the second victim.

sections.heading: The Rescue Hierarchy: Reach, Throw, Row, Go
sections.body:
Every lifeguard course and water-rescue manual teaches the same ordered sequence, and it exists for one structural reason: each step keeps the rescuer physically farther from the danger than the step before it. You move down the list only when the current option genuinely cannot reach the person, not when it merely looks slower. The ordering is not a ranking of effectiveness — it is a ranking of how much risk the rescuer absorbs, and the whole point is to spend as little of that risk as the situation actually demands.

Reach comes first. Extend anything that lengthens your arm: a paddle, a fallen branch, a boat hook, a pool skimmer pole, an oar, a towel, a belt, a shirt knotted into a line, or in the closest cases your own forearm. Get low before you extend — kneel, sit, or lie prone on the bank or dock — and brace a foot, knee, or hip against something fixed so that a sudden pull loads the anchor rather than your balance. A person fighting to keep their mouth clear of the surface can pull with startling force, often far more than their build suggests, because they are recruiting everything they have in a reflex that does not budget for anyone else's safety.

Throw comes second, and it extends your reach from roughly two metres to twenty or more. Anything buoyant and throwable works: a ring buoy, a purpose-made rescue throw bag, a closed-cell cushion, a cooler lid, a sealed empty jug or fuel can, a spare life jacket, even a coiled garden hose with a float tied to the end. Aim slightly beyond the person and upcurrent or upwind, so the object drifts down onto them; a throw that lands short but arrives is worth more than one that lands perfectly and is swept past in three seconds.

Row comes third. A canoe, kayak, rowboat, paddleboard, or even an inflatable closes the remaining distance while keeping a hull between you and the water. Approach from downwind or downstream where practical so the current carries you onto the person rather than forcing you to fight it at the moment of contact, and prefer to hand over a float or have them hold the stern rather than letting them climb over the gunwale, which capsizes small craft with remarkable ease.

Go — swimming out yourself — is last, and it is last because it is the step most likely to convert one victim into two. The honest caveat is that circumstances sometimes compress the ladder: a small child face-down two metres from a pool edge is a reach, not a debate. But the discipline of running the list in order, even quickly, is what stops the instinct to swim from overriding the three safer options that were available the whole time.

sections.heading: Why Swimming Out to Help Kills Rescuers
sections.body:
A person in the grip of the instinctive drowning response is not making decisions in any ordinary sense. Their nervous system has committed to one goal — get the mouth above the surface — and it will use whatever object arrives to do it, including a kickboard, a life ring, or a rescuer's shoulders, arms and head. This is not panic in the everyday sense of poor judgement under stress, and it cannot be talked down. It is a reflex operating below the level of deliberate thought, and it is strong enough to push a fit, trained swimmer underwater and hold them there.

The mechanism is straightforward once you see it. Anything that floats becomes a platform, and anything that floats better than the victim becomes the preferred platform. A rescuer swimming out empty-handed is, physically speaking, the most buoyant object in reach — a body with air in its lungs, actively swimming, arriving head-first into grabbing range. The victim climbs, the rescuer's head goes under, the rescuer instinctively fights back rather than releasing, and both people now have the same reflex running at the same time with no flotation between them.

This is why multiple-fatality drowning incidents cluster into one recognisable pattern. A bystander — very often a parent, sibling or friend, and frequently a competent swimmer — sees someone struggling, enters the water without any flotation, is grabbed, and goes under. In a grimly common variant the original victim survives, because the rescuer functioned as the platform they needed, while the rescuer does not. Drowning prevention agencies see this repeatedly in rivers, quarries, and unguarded beaches, and it is the single strongest argument for the reach-throw-row-go ordering.

If entering the water truly is the only remaining option, the rule that changes the odds most is simple: never go empty-handed. Take something buoyant that can be pushed out in front of you and offered at arm's length — a rescue tube, a bodyboard, a life jacket held by the straps, a fender, a sealed jug, a floating cooler. That object becomes the thing they climb, and it keeps your airway out of the transaction.
