This has little to do with the rope's rated strength: drop-test work has repeatedly severed loaded nylon rope over a sharp edge at a small fraction of its nominal breaking load, sometimes in a single shock event. Published figures scatter widely with edge radius, rope construction and how the load arrives, so no single number should be memorised as a safe threshold — the honest lesson is only that the margin you assumed is not there. Movement makes it far worse. Any bounce, swing or haul-and-reset cycle saws the same millimetre of rope back and forth across the same millimetre of stone, and the friction generates heat locally; nylon softens somewhere around two hundred and fifteen to two hundred and fifty degrees Celsius, which a fast-running rope on hard rock can reach at the contact point. Protection is ranked, not binary. A purpose-made edge roller is best because it converts sliding into rolling. Next is a smooth rounded object lashed at the lip — a length of pipe, a smooth log, a rounded pack frame — which increases the bend radius so the load spreads over centimetres instead of millimetres. Below that come canvas, carpet, a tarp or a stuffed pack, which cushion but still slide. A folded jacket is the weakest common choice: thin, slippery and easily dragged over the edge by the rope it was meant to protect. Whatever you use, tie it off independently, because padding that migrates is padding that is not there. Better still, change the geometry: move the anchor back or raise the rope's departure point so it leaves the edge at a shallower angle, or reroute so it crosses at a rounded spot rather than a fresh fracture. Inspect any rope pressed into service by milking it hand over hand through a loose fist along its whole length, feeling for flat spots, spongy or lumpy sections that indicate a broken core, sheath sliding independently of the core, glazed fused patches, and fuzz deep enough to expose core fibres. Remember also that knots themselves cost strength — a figure-eight typically retains around seventy-five to eighty percent, a bowline nearer sixty-five to seventy-five, a plain overhand less still. The genuinely invisible damage is chemical: battery acid, bleach, strong alkalis and some solvents destroy nylon with little visible change, so a rope stored beside a car battery, in a boat locker or under months of sun should be demoted to a tag line and never trusted with a person's weight.

sections.heading: When to Stop and Wait for a Trained Team
sections.body: A short set of signals marks the point where improvised rescue should stop, and recognising them early is worth more than any rigging skill. If the casualty's full weight would hang from the system rather than merely be steadied by it, that is a trained-team problem. If no anchor can be verified, or the only candidates are questionable, that is a trained-team problem, because everything downstream inherits that doubt. If the person is unconscious, has a suspected spinal injury, or cannot cooperate with their own rescue, the tolerance for error in an improvised system collapses. And if you find yourself assembling an unfamiliar or compound system under time pressure, having never built it in a calm setting, that unfamiliarity is itself the hazard. Set the abort criteria out loud before starting and give one person the explicit job of calling the stop, because escalating commitment is a documented and powerful bias: the more rope you have already rigged, the harder it becomes to walk away from rigging that is not working. Waiting has real costs and pretending otherwise helps nobody. Professional response is commonly thirty to a hundred and twenty minutes in populated areas and many hours in wilderness, and some clocks run faster than that. A person hanging motionless in a harness can deteriorate within roughly ten to thirty minutes as the leg straps restrict venous return and blood pools in the legs; a casualty lying on cold ground, immersed in water, or bleeding significantly is also on a short clock. It is worth noting that the older, dramatic advice about carefully sitting such a patient up rather than laying them flat has been substantially revised, and current guidance is not to delay laying a rescued person flat and treating them normally. Use the waiting time deliberately rather than passively. Establish voice contact if you can do so from safe ground and keep talking, because a calm person stops making the situation worse. Get insulation under and over them if reachable. Call for help immediately and give a location precise enough to act on: a grid reference, latitude and longitude to five decimal places, or a three-word address, plus an honest description of the terrain — height of the drop, angle, surface, water, access — so the team arrives with the right equipment rather than discovering the problem on scene. Mark the approach, send someone to meet them if you have the numbers, identify an open area clear of wires for a helicopter, and preserve phone battery. There are genuine exceptions where the calculus flips and immediate imperfect action beats a correct delayed one — a face-down casualty in water, a burning vehicle, a rapidly rising flood, an obstructed airway — and honest practitioners disagree at the margins. But in the ordinary case, a slower professional rescue that works reliably beats a faster improvised one that fails halfway through with two people now committed to it.

guides.title: Structural Collapse: Self-Rescue, Void Awareness, and Helping Without Becoming a Casualty
guides.summary: Most deaths after a building collapse happen in the hours that follow the initial event, not during it. This guide covers what to do if you're trapped, how search teams find people in rubble, why secondary collapse is the single biggest threat to bystanders, and what an untrained civilian can safely do at a collapse site.

sections.heading: The First Minutes After a Collapse: What Kills People Next
sections.body: The structural failure itself is only the first hazard, and often not the one that determines how many people die. What follows kills more people than most expect: secondary or progressive collapse of already-weakened structural members, fires ignited by ruptured gas lines or damaged wiring, and untrained bystanders entering unstable debris and becoming additional casualties rather than rescuers. Two medical hazards run in parallel and are worth naming precisely. The first is dust. Collapse dust is pulverised concrete, gypsum and silica, and concrete dust is strongly alkaline, typically pH 10 to 12 — chemically closer to oven cleaner than to garden soil. It burns the airway lining rather than simply irritating it, which is why the persistent 'World Trade Center cough' appeared in responders who worked unmasked for hours. The second is crush syndrome, first described by Eric Bywaters and Desmond Beall in 1941 from casualties of the London Blitz. When a large muscle mass is compressed for roughly an hour or more, the starved muscle breaks down and fills with potassium, myoglobin and phosphate. While the weight stays on, that stays trapped locally. The moment the weight comes off, it floods the circulation, and the potassium surge can stop the heart within minutes. This is why people sometimes die at the instant of rescue rather than during entrapment, and why intravenous fluids should ideally be running before the load is lifted. The timeline matters as much as the mechanism. Live rescue is overwhelmingly a first-day phenomenon: across studies of major earthquakes, most people recovered alive are reached within the first 24 hours, and the proportion found alive falls steeply on each subsequent day. Crucially, most of those early survivors are not freed by professional teams at all. After the 1980 Irpinia earthquake in Italy, roughly 90 percent of survivors were extricated by neighbours and passers-by, and similar patterns appear after Tangshan in 1976 and later events. Urban search and rescue teams typically need hours to mobilise and can take a day or more to arrive from another region. That is the uncomfortable arithmetic behind everything that follows: the people physically present in the first hour genuinely matter, and they are also the least equipped to judge what is safe. So call emergency services first, even if you intend to help while waiting, because every minute of advance notice compounds through a slow mobilisation chain. Then, before moving toward anyone, spend fifteen deliberate seconds looking: leaning or sagging sections that have not finished falling, the sulphurous mercaptan smell added to natural gas, arcing or sparking wires, smoke, water pooling where no water should be. Aftershocks follow the same statistical rules everywhere — the largest is typically about one magnitude unit below the mainshock, and they arrive most densely in the first hours. The urge to sprint in is admirable and it is also, repeatedly and measurably, how helpers become patients.

sections.heading: If You're Trapped: Conserve Air, Protect Your Airway, Signal Smart
sections.body: If you are trapped in debris, protect your airway before anything else. Pull a shirt, scarf or mask over your nose and mouth, breathe through it, and if you can wet the fabric slightly, do — damp cloth captures fine particles far better than dry. Collapse dust is not merely unpleasant; the pulverised concrete in it is caustic enough to inflame the airway, and in a confined space you will re-breathe whatever you stir up. That single fact drives the next rule: move as little as possible. Every scramble raises a fresh cloud and risks shifting material that is currently holding weight off you. Before attempting to move at all, work out by feel whether you are merely enclosed or actually pinned, and whether anything above you is resting on something that would move if you did. The gas that limits you in a tight space is usually carbon dioxide, not oxygen. A resting adult exhales roughly 0.2 litres of carbon dioxide per minute. In a genuinely sealed one-cubic-metre pocket, that is about 0.02 percent added per minute, so you would pass two percent — headache and obvious breathlessness — in a little under two hours, while oxygen would still be near 20 percent. Struggling raises your output five- to tenfold and collapses that clock proportionally. The honest caveat is that truly airtight voids are rare, because rubble is porous and leaks; the practical lesson is not to panic about suffocation but to treat calm, shallow, unhurried breathing as an actual resource you are spending. Water, not air, is the usual limit over days. Expect roughly three days without any water in warm conditions, longer when cool and still — documented rescues at seven to eleven days exist, but survivors at those extremes almost always found some water. Do not drink urine; its dissolved salt load costs you more water to excrete than it provides. Signal with structure, not with your voice. Sound travels through concrete at roughly 3,000 to 4,000 metres per second versus 343 in air, and it survives the trip far better, so tapping a pipe, a steel beam or exposed reinforcing bar with a stone or a shoe heel carries much further than a shout and costs almost no energy or water. Use a deliberate pattern — three taps, pause, three taps, pause — because a rhythm reads as intentional where irregular noise reads as settling debris. A pealess whistle produces well over 100 decibels for one breath and is worth carrying for exactly this reason. Ration shouting to short bursts. If you have a phone, switch it to aeroplane mode between attempts: with no signal it otherwise transmits at full power hunting for a tower and will flatten the battery in hours. Send text messages rather than calling — SMS needs a fraction of the signal and queues until a sliver of coverage appears.

sections.heading: The Call-and-Listen Search Pattern: How Rescuers Find Voices in the Rubble
sections.body: Urban search and rescue teams find people by hailing, a disciplined call-and-listen cycle that looks almost absurdly simple and is one of the highest-yield techniques in the discipline. Every engine, generator, saw and conversation on site stops. One searcher calls loudly and specifically — identifying themselves as rescuers and telling anyone who hears to shout or tap — and then everyone present goes completely, genuinely silent and listens. A workable civilian rhythm is roughly ten seconds of calling followed by thirty to sixty seconds of total silence, repeated about three times from one position, then the whole cycle repeated from a new position five to ten metres away and, where possible, from a different face of the pile. The repetition from multiple positions is not ritual; it compensates for how badly rubble carries airborne sound. A debris pile is a chaotic stack of slabs, timber, insulation and air gaps, and each interface reflects, absorbs and scatters sound unpredictably. A tap that is inaudible from one side of a pile can be obvious from four metres away, and a voice can be funnelled sideways along a void for twenty metres while being inaudible directly above its source. Nobody can predict those paths from the surface, so teams brute-force the problem by listening from many places rather than trusting any one negative result. Professional teams layer instruments on top of the same logic. Seismic and acoustic listening devices — the Delsar family is the common example — place sensitive geophone pads on concrete to pick up vibration transmitted through the structure itself, which is precisely why tapping beats shouting: it puts energy into the material the sensors are touching. Fibre-optic search cameras on flexible poles are threaded through drilled holes to see into voids, and live-find dogs are worked across the pile in short shifts because scent pools out of openings and a good dog covers ground far faster than a human line search. All of these still depend on the site being quiet, which is why an incident commander will halt heavy machinery for listening windows even under enormous time pressure. For anyone trapped, this is the single most useful thing to understand about how you will be found. Your best chance of being heard is not during the noisy, active phase of work but during those deliberate silent windows, which may come only every several minutes. That is the real argument for rationing your voice and your energy into short, repeated, patterned signals rather than continuous shouting: continuous shouting exhausts you within an hour and will very likely be spent entirely during periods when nobody could have heard it. If you are a bystander before teams arrive, run the simplified version honestly — get everyone to stop talking and stop moving, call once clearly, and then hold a real silence long enough to feel uncomfortable before deciding nobody answered.

sections.heading: Understanding Void Spaces
sections.body: A void is any open, unfilled pocket that forms inside collapsed debris, and voids are the entire reason anyone survives a collapse at all. Rescue doctrine names the recurring shapes because each one tells you where to look. A lean-to void forms when a floor slab fails at one end and drops, while the other end stays supported, leaving a long triangular wedge beneath the high side. A V-shaped void forms when a slab breaks in the middle and sags but both ends stay attached to their walls, leaving survivable pockets along both edges of the room. An A-frame or tent void forms when two slabs fall against each other and prop, with space beneath the apex. A pancake collapse, where floors drop flat onto one another with little lateral displacement, is the one that produces almost no voids and by far the worst survival rates — it is the signature failure of non-ductile reinforced concrete frames with weak or short columns, seen at Mexico City in 1985 and repeatedly in the 2023 Turkey and Syria earthquakes. Individual voids form beside anything rigid enough to resist crushing: stairwells, structural columns and beams, sturdy desks and dressers, refrigerators, bathtubs, and reinforced door frames. Stairwells and small bathrooms perform disproportionately well — a stairwell is usually a stiff, heavily reinforced core, and a bathroom combines short spans, plumbing walls and a cast tub. Search teams probe near these features first because that is simply where the survivable geometry is, not because of any preference for orderly searching. This is where an honest caveat is owed, because the observation is often converted into bad advice. The claim popularised as the 'triangle of life' — that in an earthquake you should lie down beside heavy furniture rather than get under it — is rejected by the American Red Cross, FEMA, the United States Geological Survey and mainstream earthquake engineers. The descriptive point is true: voids do form beside rigid objects. The prescriptive leap is not, because in an engineered building most injuries come from falling objects and flying glass rather than total collapse, and Drop, Cover and Hold On protects against the far likelier hazard while keeping you from being thrown across a moving room. The calculus genuinely differs in unreinforced masonry or non-engineered construction, where full collapse is the dominant risk and getting outside within a couple of seconds, if you truly can, is reasonable. If you are inside a void, resist the urge to enlarge it. Debris resting in an arch or a wedge is a structure, and it is carrying load through friction and point contacts you cannot see; pulling the wrong piece removes a keystone and brings the pocket down instead of opening it. Feel for a second exit rather than excavating a first one, keep your airway covered because voids concentrate dust and can accumulate leaked gas, and if you smell gas, stop any activity that could make a spark.

sections.heading: Secondary Collapse: The Biggest Threat to Untrained Helpers
sections.body: Progressive collapse — the spread of failure from one damaged element to a whole section of building — is the hazard that kills helpers, and it is worth understanding structurally rather than as a vague warning. Buildings carry weight down defined load paths: slab to beam, beam to column, column to foundation. Remove one element and its load does not disappear; it redistributes onto neighbours that may or may not have the reserve capacity to take it. The founding case is Ronan Point in London in 1968, where a modest gas explosion in an eighteenth-floor kitchen blew out one load-bearing precast wall panel, the floor above lost its support and fell, and the impact drove the corner of the building down through every storey to the ground. Four people died, the building was barely damaged elsewhere, and the event rewrote codes worldwide around structural robustness and alternate load paths. The same mechanism appears in the 1995 Alfred P. Murrah Building bombing and in the 2021 Champlain Towers South collapse at Surfside. A partially collapsed structure has, by definition, already lost some of those paths, and the survivors are carrying loads in configurations no engineer ever checked. Add the scale of the weights involved and the reluctance to improvise becomes obvious. Reinforced concrete masses about 2,400 kilograms per cubic metre, so a fairly ordinary 200-millimetre slab weighs roughly 480 kilograms for every square metre; a three-by-three-metre fragment is about four and a third tonnes. Nothing about a debris pile responds usefully to enthusiasm. The rubble itself behaves as a second, cruder structure: irregular blocks wedged against each other, holding through friction and a handful of point contacts. Pull out a piece that looks like loose clutter and you may have removed a strut. Trained teams therefore work debris slowly and incrementally, cribbing and shoring as they go, watching for movement after every removal rather than after every hour. Rain matters too — water adds weight to absorbent debris and lubricates contact surfaces — as do wind on leaning panels, aftershocks, and the vibration of heavy machinery. This is why professional response opens with a structural size-up performed by a specialist before anyone enters: what remains standing, what is likely to move, what load paths survive, and where shores must go. It is also why the standing advice to untrained bystanders is not to enter a collapsed or partially collapsed structure at all, however unbearable that feels when you know who is inside. If a person can be reached, spoken to, kept warm, given water or freed from outside the structure's footprint, that is overwhelmingly the better option than a brief trip inside — and 'brief' is a meaningless protection, because collapse takes under a second.

sections.heading: Reading a Damaged Structure Before You Go Near It
sections.body: A small number of visible signs reliably indicate that a structure is still moving, and none of them require an engineering degree to read. The first is geometry. Walls or whole sections leaning out of vertical, floor and roof lines that visibly sag or bow, and door and window openings that have gone out of square are all evidence that the frame has deformed. A useful rough threshold is that a wall out of plumb by more than about two percent of its height — roughly 60 millimetres over a three-metre storey — is seriously displaced; you can check with a weighted string or a phone's level app from a safe distance. The second is cracking, and the pattern says more than the presence. In masonry, diagonal stair-step cracks following the mortar joints indicate shear or differential settlement; cracks running straight through the bricks or blocks themselves indicate higher stress and are worse. Width gives a usable scale: the widely used building-damage categories treat cracks under about 1 millimetre as very slight, up to 5 millimetres as slight, 5 to 15 millimetres as moderate, and anything beyond roughly 15 to 25 millimetres as severe. The most alarming single sight is a column whose concrete cover has spalled away to expose reinforcing bars that have visibly buckled outward — that column has yielded and is no longer reliably carrying anything. The third is active motion. Dust still sifting from ceilings, small debris trickling, and creaking, cracking or popping sounds mean the structure is settling now, not that it finished and stabilised. Water sounds and running water can mean a broken main undermining the foundation. Utilities close the list. Natural gas is odourless, so suppliers add mercaptan precisely so leaks are smelled far below the 5 percent concentration at which gas becomes explosive; a strong smell means leave and keep others back, and do not operate switches, doorbells, torches or vehicle ignitions nearby, because any of those can spark. Treat every wire as live. Around a downed power line keep at least ten metres clear, and if you must leave an area where a line is energised, shuffle with your feet together rather than striding, because voltage falls off across the ground and a long stride can put a lethal difference between your feet. Standing water may be energised or may hide a scoured foundation or an open shaft. After a major earthquake, engineers post standard placards under the ATC-20 system: green means inspected and usable, yellow means restricted use, red means unsafe to enter. A red placard is not advice. None of these cues are subtle — the discipline they demand is simply acting on what you can plainly see instead of letting urgency override it, and reporting the specific hazard to responders rather than working around it.

sections.heading: What Untrained Civilians Can Safely Do
sections.body: There is a real and substantial role for untrained bystanders at a collapse site, and none of it involves entering an unstable structure. It is worth stating plainly because the historical record backs it: after major earthquakes, the large majority of people pulled out alive are freed by neighbours and passers-by in the first hours, before any professional team arrives. The question is never whether ordinary people matter, only which of the things they might do actually help. Locating people is the highest-value contribution. From outside the structure's footprint, run the same hail-and-listen cycle professionals use — silence everyone, call once clearly, then listen for a full thirty to sixty seconds — and report anything you hear or see with the most precise location you can give. 'Tapping, answering, from the north-east corner about four metres in from the fire escape, heard three times' is worth more to an arriving team than an hour of untargeted digging, because it converts a blind sweep of an entire pile into a directed operation. Note the time you last heard the person, too; that single detail shapes triage decisions. Beyond that, you can clear light, obviously non-structural surface debris — broken glass, loose boards, small rubble — from ground already cleared of casualties, opening working space for treatment and extraction, provided you stay well away from anything that could be carrying load. You can give first aid to people already freed, which is frequently more urgently needed than more hands on the pile. Direct pressure controls most bleeding; a tourniquet goes high and tight on the limb, roughly five to eight centimetres above the wound and never over a joint, tightened until bleeding stops and the pulse beyond it disappears, with the time of application written down. Improvised tourniquets fail often, and the usual reasons are a band narrower than about four centimetres and no rigid windlass to generate real pressure. Where several people are hurt, the START method sorts them fast: anyone walking is low priority; among the rest, a breathing rate over thirty, absent radial pulse, or inability to follow a simple command marks someone as immediate. One warning deserves special emphasis. If a person has been pinned under heavy weight across a large muscle mass for more than roughly an hour, say so loudly to arriving medics before the weight comes off, because sudden release can flood the circulation with potassium and stop the heart, and fluids started beforehand change that outcome. Finally, the unglamorous jobs are genuinely valuable: acting as a runner between the pile and arriving units, keeping a written list of who is accounted for and who is missing, keeping access routes clear, and turning a milling crowd into an organised group. Wear gloves, eye protection, a dust mask and closed boots if you have them, and drink water — none of this requires entering a compromised structure, and all of it directly helps.

sections.heading: What NOT to Do Around a Collapsed Structure
sections.body: Do not enter a collapsed or visibly damaged structure to search, whatever the personal stake, unless you have the training and equipment for it. This bears repeating because it is both the most common and the most lethal bystander mistake, and because 'just for a second' offers no protection when the event you are risking takes under a second to happen. Do not remove debris quickly, and never by hauling on the most accessible piece. If you clear anything at all, work from stable ground outside the footprint, one piece at a time, pausing after each to watch and listen for settling. Do not climb onto a debris pile for a better view or to reach someone; the pile is held together by friction at contact points you cannot see, and your added weight redistributes those loads in ways nobody can predict from the surface. Do not assume that a structure which survived the initial event has therefore stabilised — progressive collapses characteristically happen after a pause, sometimes hours later, which is exactly what makes them so effective at catching helpers. Do not create ignition sources. No open flame, no smoking, no operating switches, doorbells, torch buttons or vehicle ignitions near a site where gas may have leaked; natural gas becomes explosive at concentrations around 5 to 15 percent in air, and a spark is enough. Do not touch or move wires, and do not step into standing water near a damaged building. Do not block access. Fire apparatus needs a clear lane roughly six metres wide, and aerial and heavy rescue units need substantial set-up space; private vehicles converging on a scene routinely delay the equipment that actually matters more than the extra hands compensate for. In the same spirit, do not fly a hobby drone over the site — it has repeatedly grounded medical helicopters at real disasters — and do not tie up emergency lines with repeat calls that add no new information. Do not move someone with a suspected spinal injury unless leaving them is the greater danger, do not remove an impaled object, and do not loosen a tourniquet once it is on. Be cautious about pushing food or water through debris to a trapped person without telling responders: someone who may need surgery or who cannot swallow safely in their position can aspirate, and the medical team needs to know what has gone in. Finally, do not ignore your own condition. Dehydration, exhaustion, cuts through thin shoes, and hours of unprotected dust exposure are how helpers become patients — and the long-term respiratory illness among unmasked World Trade Center responders is the honest reminder that some of that cost arrives years later. And when an incident commander tells you to leave an area, leave; the scene is under unified command precisely so that one person is tracking the hazards nobody standing at the pile can see.

sections.heading: Marking and Communicating With Professional Responders
sections.body: Search teams mark buildings because memory and radio traffic fail at scale. On a site with a dozen structures, three shifts and teams from different agencies, the only reliable way to stop people re-searching cleared ground is to write the answer on the building itself, in a form that survives rain, darkness and a change of personnel. The United States urban search and rescue system uses two distinct markings, and confusing them is the usual error. The structure and hazard marking is a roughly 600-millimetre square box in international orange spray paint at the main point of entry, recording who assessed the building, when, what hazards exist inside, and whether entry is permitted; a circle drawn around the box with 'NE' means do not enter. The search marking is different: a single diagonal slash is painted as a team goes in, and a second slash crossing it to form an X is painted only as they come out. That distinction is the whole point — a lone slash means a team is still inside. The four quadrants of the completed X carry the team's identifier, the time and date they exited, the hazards found, and the count of victims, conventionally live and dead recorded separately, with a zero meaning genuinely none. A separate victim marking, a large V, flags where someone is believed to be, circled once the victim is confirmed and struck through once removed. The honest caveat is that this is not a single global standard: the INSARAG system used for international deployments differs in shape and content, so read markings you encounter as information, and do not invent new ones. As a civilian, do not attempt the official symbols. Do the same job in plain language: with a marker, chalk or a piece of tape at the entry, write your name or group, the time, what you checked, and what you found — 'checked ground floor and front rooms 14:20, one person removed, elderly man believed still in rear bedroom' is enormously useful and unambiguous. The handover to arriving professionals is worth rehearsing, because people reliably do it badly under stress. Lead with operational facts in a fixed order, which is exactly what structured models such as METHANE exist to enforce: the exact location, the type of incident, the hazards you have observed, how to get in, how many casualties and their rough condition, and what is needed. Add what has already been searched and who is known to be unaccounted for. Keep it to under a minute. The urge to narrate the experience is human and completely understandable, but the crew in front of you is building a picture under time pressure, and a calm, ordered, factual thirty seconds measurably speeds up everything that happens next. If networks are congested, text rather than call — messages need far less signal and queue until they get through.

sections.heading: CERT and Preparing Before Disaster Strikes
sections.body: Community Emergency Response Team programmes exist precisely to close the gap between wanting to help and knowing how. The idea came out of a hard lesson: the Los Angeles City Fire Department created the model in 1985, informed by the Mexico City earthquake that year, in which large numbers of spontaneous untrained volunteers were themselves killed attempting rescues. FEMA adopted and nationalised the curriculum in 1993, and there are now thousands of local programmes, with equivalents run by emergency management agencies in many other countries. The basic course is typically around twenty hours spread over seven to nine sessions, and it is usually free. The syllabus maps almost exactly onto the hazards a collapse presents: disaster preparedness and hazard identification; fire safety and how to shut off utilities; disaster medical operations, covering airway, severe bleeding and shock, then triage using the START method; light search and rescue, including size-up, systematic searching, and cribbing and simple leverage to lift weight off a trapped person; team organisation and documentation; and disaster psychology, which matters more than people expect for staying functional and keeping others calm. The word 'light' is doing real work in that list. CERT explicitly trains volunteers to operate only in lightly damaged structures and to mark, report and stay out of anything moderately or heavily damaged. The training's most valuable output is not a technique but a boundary — the judgement to recognise which side of the line a given situation sits on. Preparation at home is the other half. Learn where your gas and water shut-offs are and keep the right tool beside them; the gas valve is turned a quarter turn so the lug lies across the pipe, and it takes an adjustable spanner or a meter key, not fingers. Shut gas off only if you smell or hear it or see obvious damage, because only the utility may safely restore service and relight appliances, and after a regional disaster that can take weeks. Strap your water heater top and bottom; it is both a falling hazard and, at roughly 150 to 300 litres, a serious emergency water reserve. Keep a kit somewhere you can reach when the building cannot be entered — a car, garage or shed rather than a bedroom cupboard. Leather gloves, an N95 or P100 respirator, sealed goggles, a hard hat, boots stiff enough to resist a nail, a headlamp with spare cells, a pealess whistle, a pry bar, a marker, a tourniquet and pressure dressing, and about four litres of water per person per day. Agree a household plan with two meeting points and an out-of-area contact, since long-distance circuits often survive when local ones jam. Then reduce the odds you need any of it: anchor tall furniture to studs, latch cabinets, and move heavy objects to low shelves, because in most earthquakes it is falling contents, not collapsing buildings, that hurt people. The people who handle a real collapse well are consistently those who already knew, calmly and in advance, where the line sits between helping and becoming one more person who has to be found.
